title: Below the Water Table: Water That Lifts, Leaks and Attacks
summary: Groundwater does three things to a slab below the water table: it lifts it, leaks through it and attacks it chemically, and each is governed by a different document, often handled by a different person. All three are decided on the day of the pour, so they are settled in design.
body:
Mr Shabazz, below the water table a slab faces three separate threats, uplift, leakage and chemical attack, and each has its own rulebook and often its own specialist. All three are one-way doors that close when the concrete is placed.

In plain English

When the lowest floor of a building sits below groundwater, water pushes up on it, seeps through any crack or joint, and carries dissolved salts that can attack concrete and reinforcement. Uplift is a structural problem for the structural engineer, leakage a waterproofing problem for the envelope designer, and chemical attack a durability problem for whoever specifies the concrete mix. Because three people handle them, it is easy for one to fall between them.

Leakage: dampproofing or waterproofing

The IBC distinguishes dampproofing, which resists moisture without water pressure, from waterproofing, which resists water under hydrostatic pressure. In recent editions the dampproofing and waterproofing section, commonly Section 1805, requires waterproofing where a groundwater investigation shows a hydrostatic pressure condition and no groundwater control system holds the water down, with lowering of about 5 feet, 1.5 metres, below the floor commonly quoted as the control threshold [unverified — confirm independently]. Dampproofing over a high water table is a defect, however well it is installed.

Uplift: a load, not a nuisance

ASCE 7 treats groundwater pressure as a load. When checking uplift, the building's dead weight is counted at a reduced factor, commonly quoted at about 0.9, because overestimating the weight holding the slab down is the unsafe direction [unverified — confirm independently]. The governing case is often the empty building, or the day the pumps stop.

Durability: exposure categories

ACI 318 assigns exposure categories: F for freezing and thawing, S for sulfate, W for contact with water and C for corrosion of reinforcement. They are set from tested soil and groundwater chemistry, and they fix limits such as maximum water to cementitious materials ratio, minimum strength and cement type. Commonly quoted figures for moderate sulfate exposure are a maximum ratio of about 0.50 with about 4,000 pounds per square inch minimum strength, and for severe about 0.45 and 4,500 [unverified — confirm independently]. A default exposure class chosen without tests is a guess about chemistry nobody measured.

Which slabs ACI 318 covers

A structural mat is within ACI 318's scope. Many ordinary ground slabs that do not transmit structural loads fall instead to the IBC Chapter 19 minimum provisions and to ACI 302.1R and 302.2R, guides that bind only if specified. Vapour retarder materials are classed under ASTM E1745 and installed under ASTM E1643, and ACI 301 sets temperature limits for mass concrete when the specification cites it [unverified — confirm independently].

How mats and ground slabs fail below water

The mechanisms recur. Uplift, when pumps stop on the programme date rather than the certified crossover. Thermal cracking in thick mats, where the hot core and cooling surface pull apart, covered by ACI 207 mass concrete guidance [unverified — confirm independently]. Shrinkage cracking and curling from late saw cuts and missing curing. And punctured vapour retarders or membranes, damaged by reinforcement chairs or boots before the pour. The organisational failure behind them is that each symptom is repaired on its own, by someone with no authority over the whole slab.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical building with a mat whose base sits 1.5 metres below grade, and groundwater measured over a season at 0.5 metres below grade.

  1. Leakage: head at the base is 1.0 metre, and the design includes no permanent groundwater control. Hydrostatic pressure exists, so waterproofing, not dampproofing, is required. The specification currently shows dampproofing: correct it before tender.
  2. Uplift: 1.0 metre of head is about 10 kilopascals. An 0.8 metre mat weighs about 19.2 kilopascals, about 17.3 at a 0.9 factor. It resists uplift empty. Had the base been 3 metres deep, the head would be 2.5 metres and the empty mat would float.
  3. Durability: groundwater tests show elevated sulfates. The engineer assigns the matching sulfate class, which sets a lower maximum water to cementitious ratio, a higher minimum strength and a sulfate-resisting binder. The default mix in the draft specification met none of these.
  4. All three changes cost little at design stage. After the pour, they cost a membrane that cannot be reached, an anchored or ballasted mat, or a concrete whose durability cannot be improved.

Joints and penetrations

Most leaks below the water table come through the places where the slab is interrupted: construction joints between pours, joints between slab and wall, and penetrations for pipes and cables. Each needs a detail: a waterstop across the joint, a sealed sleeve around each pipe, and a membrane lapped and bonded around every interruption. Ask for those details on a drawing, not in a general note, and make them hold points before the concrete covers them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the gap between three specialists: the structural engineer checks uplift, the envelope designer specifies the membrane, the specifier picks a mix, and nobody checks that all three used the same groundwater level and chemistry.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relies on a single groundwater reading from the day of drilling, which may miss the seasonal high, and lets the concrete mix default to a standard class without testing the water.

How you will use it

Require a design groundwater level from monitoring over time, and make all three specialists work from it. Confirm waterproofing rather than dampproofing wherever hydrostatic pressure exists. Ask for the uplift check in the empty condition and the certified pumps-off date. Require soil and water chemistry tests and an exposure class derived from them. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer, structural engineer of record, waterproofing designer and concrete specifier.
checklist: Set one design groundwater level from monitoring over time and give it to every specialist.
Specify waterproofing, not dampproofing, wherever hydrostatic pressure exists.
Ask for the uplift check with the building empty.
Get the date pumps may stop certified in writing.
Test soil and groundwater chemistry and derive the exposure class from the results.
Protect membranes and vapour retarders from damage before the pour.
Check that the structural, waterproofing and mix designs use the same groundwater data.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A draft specification shows dampproofing under a basement slab, a standard concrete mix, and dewatering ending at slab completion. Groundwater sits 1 metre above the slab base and tests show sulfates. What three things are wrong?
selftest.a: Dampproofing is wrong where there is hydrostatic pressure and no permanent groundwater control; waterproofing is required (IBC dampproofing and waterproofing provisions, verify against the adopted edition). The mix must follow the sulfate exposure class derived from the test results under ACI 318. And the pumps-off date must follow a certified uplift check in the empty condition, not slab completion.

apply: For a hypothetical basement slab with its base 2 metres below the water table, list what you would ask each of the three specialists, using one sentence each.
sources: IBC dampproofing and waterproofing provisions (commonly Section 1805), ASCE 7 load combinations, ACI 318 exposure categories, ACI 301, ACI 207, ACI 302.1R and 302.2R, ASTM E1745 and E1643 as commonly cited; thresholds, factors and limits vary by edition [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical.

title: Pour Day: Hold Points From Formation to Slab, and the Mat Pour Go or No-Go
summary: Everything that decides foundation and ground slab quality happens before the concrete arrives, so the owner's control is a short set of hold points sampled on an element he chooses. A large mat is poured once over a membrane never seen again, and its readiness review is a go or no-go decision made the day before.
body:
Mr Shabazz, below-ground concrete is decided the day before it is poured, at the steps that will be buried. The owner's control is a handful of hold points, and for a large mat, a readiness review that says go or no-go before the first truck is ordered.

In plain English

Footings, mats and ground slabs are built in a sequence where each step is covered by the next: the bearing soil by blinding, the membrane by reinforcement, the reinforcement and services by concrete. Once covered, nothing can be checked without breaking it out. So quality control means stopping the work in front of each step until someone has looked and written it down.

Building a footing, in order

The formation is trimmed without churning the bearing soil. The geotechnical engineer or special inspector accepts it, under the IBC soils special inspection provisions, and soft or unexpected material is treated as a differing site condition, not trimmed out quietly [unverified — confirm independently]. Blinding is placed the same day. Reinforcement goes on chairs to the required cover, commonly quoted at about 75 millimetres for concrete cast against earth under ACI 318 [unverified — confirm independently], with column starter bars set by template and checked by survey. Cast-in items from other trades are fixed. The pour follows, with sampling under ASTM C31 and C39 and proper curing. Backfill goes in compacted, tested layers.

The ground slab sequence

Proof-roll the subgrade and accept it. Place and compact the sub-base, and test every service trench backfill by location, because the crack along the drain line comes from a hurried trench. Pressure-test underground services before burial. Lay the vapour retarder, ASTM E1745 material installed to ASTM E1643, lapped and sealed, and check it before reinforcement and again before the pour. Place reinforcement on chairs, isolation joints and the pour card. Pour with sampling and no added water. Finish, saw cut on time and cure, and measure flatness, commonly within about 72 hours under ACI 117 and ASTM E1155. Finally test moisture to the flooring manufacturer's method, ASTM F2170 or F1869, before flooring goes down [unverified — confirm independently for every standard and edition].

The owner's hold points

Under Design-Build, the owner requires the inspection and test plan and samples it on an element he chooses. Four hold points carry most of the value: formation accepted; reinforcement and starter bars released; pour card signed by every trade with cast-in items; underground services tested. For the slab, add vapour retarder checked before the pour and moisture results before flooring. Never sign them yourself or direct the fix.

The mat pour

A mat is poured once, over a membrane no one will see again, under every column. Three things decide its quality. Continuity: fresh concrete placed against concrete that has begun to set leaves a cold joint, so either every face is kept live or the pour stops at a joint the engineer located, with a waterstop. Supply: plant output, trucks, haul time, the pump's real rate and the crew. Heat: the core heats up as cement hydrates while the surface cools, and the difference causes thermal cracking; ACI 301 limits for mass concrete are commonly quoted at about 70 degrees Celsius maximum and about 19 degrees core to surface, with ACI 207 as guidance [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example

Take a hypothetical mat 32 by 24 metres, 0.8 metres thick.

  1. Volume: 32 times 24 times 0.8 is about 614 cubic metres.
  2. At a real pump rate of 45 cubic metres an hour, about 13.7 hours of continuous placing.
  3. At 8 cubic metres a truck, about 77 loads, arriving about 5.6 an hour, one every 11 minutes, for nearly 14 hours.
  4. Delivery time from batching to discharge, commonly quoted at about 90 minutes under ASTM C94 [unverified — confirm independently], limits how far the plant can be from the site in traffic.
  5. Cylinder sets at a commonly quoted one per 150 cubic yards, about 115 cubic metres: 614 divided by 115 is about 5.3, so at least 6 sets.
  6. Readiness questions the day before: is there a standby pump on site, a second batching plant committed, a retarder approved in case of delay, lighting for a night finish, a thermal control plan with sensors, and a named person who decides to stop at a planned joint?
  7. If the answer is one plant and no standby pump, the plan is a single point of failure for 14 hours. Either add redundancy or split the mat into two or three pours at engineer-located joints with waterstops.

The choice between one pour and several is the engineer's and the contractor's; the owner sees that it was made deliberately.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is commercial pressure on pour day. Concrete is ordered, the pump is booked, the crew is waiting, and every incentive points towards starting whether or not the readiness questions have answers.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks the concrete delivery tickets and not the membrane beneath them. The pour card signed after the pour is the same mistake in paper form.

How you will use it

Require the ITP with the hold points above and sample them on an element you choose. For a large mat, require a pour plan and a readiness review the day before, covering supply redundancy, joints, thermal control and who may stop the pour. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record, special inspector and the contractor's concrete specialist.
checklist: Hold the pour until formation, reinforcement, cast-in items and services are released in writing.
Treat soft or unexpected material at formation as a differing site condition.
Check the vapour retarder before reinforcement and again before the pour.
Test every service trench backfill by location.
For a mat, require a pour plan and a readiness review the day before.
Confirm a standby pump, committed supply, retarder and planned joint locations.
Require moisture test results before flooring is installed.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: The day before a 600 cubic metre mat pour, you learn there is one batching plant, no standby pump and no thermal plan. The contractor wants to proceed because everything is booked. What do you do?
selftest.a: Ask in writing for the readiness review to be completed before the pour: a standby pump, a second committed supply or engineer-located joints with waterstops, an approved retarder, a thermal control plan and a named person authorised to stop. At about 14 hours of continuous placing, one plant and one pump is a single point of failure. Under Design-Build, require the plan; do not direct the method.

apply: For a hypothetical mat of your own dimensions, compute volume, pouring hours at 40 cubic metres an hour, truck loads at 8 cubic metres, the truck interval, and cylinder sets at one per 115 cubic metres.
sources: IBC special inspection provisions, ACI 318 cover, ACI 301 and ACI 207 for mass concrete, ACI 117, ASTM C31, C39, C94, E1155, E1745, E1643, F2170 and F1869 as commonly cited; verify every standard, figure and edition [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical.

title: The Floor on the Ground: Support, Joints and a Point Load at the Corner
summary: A slab on grade is never better than its subgrade, and uniform support matters more than strong support. The code sets a low floor for it, joints decide where it cracks, and the same point load can pass in the middle of a panel and fail at its corner.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a ground-floor slab is a foundation, not a finish, and it cracks where its support changes, not where its support is weak. The code says little about it, so the slab is governed by what the design team writes down.

In plain English

A slab on grade rests on the ground across its whole area. It has four layers: the subgrade, the natural or filled ground; a compacted granular sub-base; a vapour retarder; and the concrete slab with its joints. Because the ground supports it everywhere, a slab can carry heavy loads, but it is never better than the subgrade beneath it, and a soft patch next to a hard one is what cracks it.

How it carries load

The classical model, from Westergaard, treats the slab as a plate on springs, with spring stiffness given by the modulus of subgrade reaction, k. As with mats, k is not a soil property; it should come from the geotechnical engineer for this slab. A slab fails in bending, and the worst places are panel corners, then edges, then the interior, because a corner has the least concrete around it to share the load.

Joints decide where it cracks

Concrete shrinks as it dries, and because it dries from the top, it also curls at the edges. Joints control where the resulting cracks form. Isolation joints separate the slab from columns, walls and pits so it can move independently. Contraction joints, usually saw cuts, create planned weak lines. Construction joints are where one day's pour meets the next. Commonly quoted guide figures put contraction joint spacing at about 24 to 36 times slab thickness, panels close to square with the long side no more than about 1.5 times the short, and saw cuts about a quarter of the depth, made within hours of finishing [unverified — confirm independently].

What the code requires

Very little. In recent editions, the IBC Chapter 19 minimum slab provisions require a slab of at least 3.5 inches, about 89 millimetres, and a vapour retarder commonly quoted as 6-mil polyethylene with 6-inch laps; ACI 302.2R guidance commonly recommends at least 10-mil under moisture-sensitive flooring, with materials classed under ASTM E1745. ACI 318 generally excludes slabs on ground unless they transmit vertical loads or lateral forces from the structure, so you must know in writing which kind you have. ACI 360R, 302.1R and 302.2R bind only when specified. Flatness and levelness live in ACI 117, measured as F-numbers under ASTM E1155. Accessibility under ICC A117.1 commonly limits changes in level to a quarter inch vertical, or up to half an inch bevelled, so settlement at a threshold becomes a compliance problem. The IBC soils chapter adds grading away from the foundation, commonly quoted at 5 percent for 10 feet, and a test-based definition of expansive soil [unverified — confirm independently for every provision]. The code is a floor, not a design.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical 150 millimetre slab of 28 megapascal concrete on a subgrade with k of 40 megapascals per metre, a placeholder value that must come from the geotechnical engineer.

  1. Joint spacing at 24 to 36 times 150 millimetres: 3.6 to 5.4 metres. Saw cut depth about a quarter: about 38 millimetres.
  2. Modulus of rupture, the concrete's bending strength, at about 0.62 times the square root of 28: about 3.28 megapascals, under the ACI 318 relationship as commonly quoted. With a guide-practice safety factor of 2, the allowable bending stress is about 1.64 megapascals.
  3. A piece of plant stands on a leg carrying 20 kilonewtons through a 150 millimetre base plate. By Westergaard's method, the radius of relative stiffness is about 650 millimetres.
  4. Stress with the leg in the middle of a panel: about 1.35 megapascals. That passes.
  5. Near a free corner: about 1.77. At a free edge: about 2.08. Both fail. Same slab, same load; only the position changed.
  6. Fixes: a 200 millimetre slab brings the three to about 0.78, 1.06 and 1.21, all passing; load transfer across joints with dowels reduces edge and corner stress; or, usually cheapest, an isolated, designed plant base.
  7. Halve k under one panel, to 20. Interior stress rises only about 6 percent, to about 1.43, but deflection rises about 40 percent, from about 0.15 to 0.21 millimetres. Stress forgives soft ground; movement does not, which is why uniform support beats strong support.

Applied to a piled frame

Under a piled frame on soft clay, columns, cores and lift pits stay put while a slab on grade settles with the ground. The slab drops away from them, opening steps at thresholds and lift sills. Choose deliberately between treating the ground, isolating the slab and accepting movement, or suspending the ground floor on the piles.

Curing and timing

Two hours often decide a slab's appearance for life. Saw cuts made too late, after the concrete has already cracked randomly, arrive after the crack has chosen its own line. Curing skipped on a hot or windy day lets the top dry faster than the bottom and increases curl at every joint. Both are cheap to control and impossible to correct, so record the finishing time, the saw-cut times by joint, and the curing method on the pour record.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is non-uniform support: an untested trench backfill or a soft patch beside firm ground. It does not show at handover, and it cracks the slab along exactly the line where the support changes.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner lets heavy plant sit on an ordinary slab, often near an edge, because the slab looks thick and the load looks small. The check that matters is the one at the actual position of each leg.

How you will use it

Ask which slabs ACI 318 covers; get k from the geotechnical engineer; check joint layout and saw-cut timing; give heavy plant isolated bases; and decide deliberately how the ground floor relates to a piled frame. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.
checklist: Get the modulus of subgrade reaction for this slab from the geotechnical engineer.
Confirm in writing whether each slab falls under ACI 318 or the code minimums.
Check joint spacing, panel proportions and saw-cut timing in the specification.
Specify the vapour retarder thickness for the actual flooring, not the code minimum.
Give heavy plant an isolated, designed base.
Decide deliberately how a slab on grade meets a piled frame.
Check thresholds and lift sills against accessibility level-change limits.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A tenant's equipment, about 20 kilonewtons per leg, is to be installed against a slab edge on an ordinary 150 millimetre slab. The interior check passed. Is it safe?
selftest.a: Not on that basis. The same load produces much higher stress at an edge or corner than in the middle of a panel; on the hypothetical numbers about 2.08 megapascals at the edge against an allowable of about 1.64. Ask the structural engineer to check the actual position, and consider an isolated base, load transfer across the joint, or relocation.

apply: For a slab thickness of your choice, compute the contraction joint spacing range at 24 to 36 times thickness and the saw-cut depth at a quarter of the thickness.
sources: Westergaard plate theory is a classical method; real designs may use other methods. IBC Chapters 18 and 19, ACI 318, 360R, 302.1R, 302.2R, ACI 117, ASTM E1155 and E1745, and ICC A117.1 as commonly cited; every provision and figure to be verified against the current adopted edition [unverified — confirm independently]. All figures hypothetical; k is a placeholder.

title: When the Floor Moves: Slab Failures and Who Pays After Handover
summary: A slab failure is a slow argument between trades, with five families of cause that mostly involve the trades around the concrete. Defects tend to appear after handover, so the owner's protection depends on the correction period, warranties he can actually enforce, and records kept as conditions of payment.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a frame failure is an event; a slab failure is a slow argument between trades that starts after the contractor has left. Your protection is decided by the records you required and the warranties you can reach, not by how strongly you feel on the day the tenant calls.

In plain English

Ground-floor slabs fail gradually: cracks, curling edges, steps at thresholds, flooring lifting. Usually several trades contributed, and each can point at another. Because the problems appear months after completion, when the contractor has gone and a tenant is complaining, the contract terms and records you put in place earlier decide whether anyone has to come back.

The five failure families

Support that moves: untested fill, or hurried service-trench backfill, settles under the slab; a crack running along the line of a drain is the trench reporting how it was backfilled. Support that changes: expansive clay swells and shrinks with moisture, and a leaking pipe can lift one spot; regions with expansive soils wrote this into design through the Post-Tensioning Institute slab-on-ground method. Reactive fill: pyrite in crushed rock fill can oxidise and expand, heaving slabs and walls, as reported in Teesside in England in the 1970s and in Ireland, where many homes built roughly from the late 1990s to 2008, mainly around Dublin, were affected; a government panel reported in 2012 and a statutory remediation scheme followed in 2013. A defect appearing in many buildings at once points to a shared supplier. Concrete that curls and cracks when saw cuts come the next morning and curing is skipped. Moisture rising through the slab and destroying adhesive-bonded flooring, defended by a proper vapour retarder and testing to ASTM F2170 or F1869 as the flooring manufacturer requires [unverified — confirm independently]. And unplanned loads, such as plant set on an ordinary slab.

Cases summarised from public accounts; read the primary reports before quoting them.

The forensic questions

Four questions sort most slab failures: what was it designed for, what was it built on, when was it cut and cured, and what was done to it afterwards. Three of the four are about the trades around the concrete, which is why nobody owns the failure.

Three windows of protection

First, completion: before final payment, defective work is simply unfinished work, and your leverage is the unpaid balance and retention. Second, the correction period: in AIA A201 as long drafted, the contractor must correct defective work for one year from substantial completion, a duty to return that is generally not written to cut short the owner's other rights [unverified — confirm independently]. Third, your general rights afterwards, limited by statutes of limitation and repose that vary by jurisdiction.

Warranties you can actually use

A flooring warranty is a promise with conditions, usually a moisture test within the manufacturer's limit before installation: no record, no claim. Subcontractor and manufacturer warranties may be out of your reach unless they are assigned to you, because you have no contract with those parties. And contractor liability insurance commonly excludes the cost of repairing the contractor's own defective work, so do not assume the insurer pays.

A worked example

Fourteen months after handover, a hypothetical ground floor under a piled frame shows four complaints: steps at two column positions, a crack along the drain run, vinyl lifting in one unit, and a cracked slab corner under a piece of plant.

  1. One cause links the steps and the crack: a slab on settling ground beside piled columns, with a hurried trench backfill. The design did not isolate or support the slab deliberately.
  2. The vinyl: no moisture test record was filed. The flooring manufacturer's warranty is likely void, and the moisture condition may relate to a punctured retarder.
  3. The plant corner: the owner's own tenant installed it on an ordinary slab. That one stays with the owner.
  4. The correction period has ended. Under Design-Bid-Build the owner may face a split between designer and contractor; under Design-Build, single-point responsibility helps only if the brief stated slab movement and moisture limits.
  5. The records that would have settled it: compaction tests by trench location, retarder inspection, saw-cut times, and moisture results.

The negotiation thread

Concede on the form of security, accepting a defects bond in exchange for lower retention, and on a reasonable liability cap that does not limit defects. Hold on warranty assignments to you, slab records as conditions of final payment, a correction obligation that restarts for corrected work, and a workable notice procedure. Retention percentages and periods are commercial practice or local statute, not standards.

Records that settle the argument

The records worth keeping are few: subgrade acceptance, compaction tests by location including every trench, the vapour retarder inspection before the pour, saw-cut times against finishing time, curing method and duration, flatness results, and the moisture test before flooring. With them, the four forensic questions have documented answers and the argument becomes short. Without them, each trade's account is as good as another's, and the owner pays for the experts.

Keep them with the building, not with the contractor. A slab problem may surface after a sale or a refinancing, when the original team is long gone, and a buyer's surveyor will ask for exactly these documents.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying the final account without the records and assignments. Once the balance is paid, the owner's main leverage is gone and the evidence that would have allocated the defect may never be produced.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes every defect is the contractor's. Some belong to the designer, some to the owner's own tenants or later works, and arguing the wrong case wastes the correction period.

How you will use it

Make slab records and warranty assignments conditions of final payment, and diarise the correction period. Professional sign-off required: construction counsel, structural engineer, and a forensic engineer for any investigation.
checklist: Make compaction, retarder, saw-cut and moisture records conditions of final payment.
Require subcontractor and manufacturer warranties to be assigned to you.
Diarise the end of the correction period and inspect before it.
State slab movement and moisture limits in any Design-Build brief.
Ask the four forensic questions before assigning blame for a slab defect.
Do not assume the contractor's liability insurer pays for defective work.
Keep owner-installed loads off ordinary slabs without an engineer's check.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Vinyl flooring is lifting in a ground-floor unit a year after handover and the flooring manufacturer asks for the pre-installation moisture test. None was filed. What does that mean, and what should you have required?
selftest.a: The warranty is probably unenforceable, because it was conditional on a moisture test within the manufacturer's limit. You should have required the test, to ASTM F2170 or F1869 as the manufacturer specifies (verify editions), as a hold point before flooring and as a condition of final payment, together with an assignment of the flooring warranty to you.

apply: Draft a three-line list of slab records you would make conditions of final payment on a hypothetical building.
sources: Post-Tensioning Institute slab-on-ground design method; pyrite cases in Teesside and Ireland summarised from public accounts, including the Irish Pyrite Panel report of 2012; AIA A201 correction period as commonly drafted; ASTM F2170 and F1869. Verify all editions and jurisdiction-specific limitation periods [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical and composite.

title: Week Eight Review and Course Close: The Lowest Floor and the Whole Building
summary: Six scenario questions on wet ground, the mat pour, slabs on grade and defects after handover, followed by a recap of the whole course. The thread through every week is that the owner's risk is fixed early, in documents and decisions that are cheap to get right and expensive to reverse.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week finished at the lowest floor, where water, concrete and trades meet. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer, then read the course recap at the end.

Question 1. Groundwater sits 1 metre above a basement slab base, there is no permanent groundwater control, and the specification shows dampproofing. What is wrong?

Answer. Hydrostatic pressure exists, so the IBC dampproofing and waterproofing provisions require waterproofing, not dampproofing (verify against the adopted edition). Check uplift in the empty condition with dead load at a reduced factor, set the concrete exposure class from tested water chemistry, and make all three specialists use the same monitored groundwater level.

Question 2. A 614 cubic metre mat is to be poured at 45 cubic metres an hour from one plant with one pump. What do you ask the day before?

Answer. That is about 14 hours of continuous placing, about 77 truck loads at one every 11 minutes. Ask for a standby pump, committed second supply or engineer-located joints with waterstops, an approved retarder, a thermal control plan, lighting, at least six cylinder sets, and a named person authorised to stop. Under Design-Build, require the plan; do not direct the pour.

Question 3. A pour card for a footing is signed the day after the concrete delivery tickets. What does it tell you?

Answer. The hold point did not work as a hold point: the check was recorded after the step it was meant to precede, so nobody knows whether cast-in items were in place. Raise it in writing with the contractor's quality manager, increase sampling, and treat it as a system failure, not a paperwork slip.

Question 4. A 20 kilonewton plant leg passes the interior check on a 150 millimetre slab. The tenant wants to place it at a free corner. Is it still fine?

Answer. No. Corner stress is higher than interior stress for the same load; on the course's hypothetical numbers about 1.77 against an allowable of about 1.64. Ask the engineer to check the real position and consider an isolated base, load transfer or a different location.

Question 5. Ground-floor slabs in several separate buildings on one development begin to heave at about the same time. Many findings or one?

Answer. Probably one: a defect appearing in many buildings at once points to a shared cause, often a shared fill supplier, as in the reactive pyrite cases reported in Ireland. Test the fill, trace its source, and handle it as one investigation.

Question 6. A year and two months after handover, flooring lifts, there is no moisture test record, and the flooring subcontractor's warranty was never assigned to you. What has gone wrong?

Answer. The correction period has probably ended, the manufacturer's warranty is probably void for want of a moisture record, and the subcontractor warranty may be out of reach without an assignment. The records and assignments should have been conditions of final payment. Take construction counsel's advice on what rights remain.

Notice that the six answers all point at the same moment: before something is buried, poured or paid. That is when the owner still has leverage and when the evidence can still be gathered.

Recap of the week

Below the water table, water lifts, leaks and attacks, and each threat has its own document and specialist. Waterproofing where pressure exists, uplift checked empty, exposure class from tested chemistry, and one groundwater level for all three.

Concrete below ground is decided at the steps that get buried. Four hold points carry most of the value, plus the retarder and the moisture test for slabs. A mat pour needs continuity, supply and thermal control, and a readiness review the day before.

A slab on grade cracks where support changes. The code sets a low floor; joints, k, retarder thickness and plant bases are design decisions. The same load passes in the middle and fails at the corner.

Slab failures are arguments between trades that surface after handover. The owner's protection is records and warranty assignments made conditions of final payment.

Recap of the course

Weeks One and Two: the delivery method allocates risk; the contract documents bind as a stack; submittals and changes are where design meets reality; quantities, the critical path and the price of a week turn a price and a date into checkable numbers; and one datum governs every level. Weeks Three and Four: the investigation must fit the foundation proposed; ground works fail in recognisable ways; the code binds as adopted; a ground baseline turns surprises into measurements; and the hole, its water and its lender all peak in risk at once. Week Five: a finished building can be lost through thin equity, the wrong debt, a tripped covenant or a misaligned partner. Week Six: temporary works are real structures, and the question is who signed the permit and what evidence was attached. Weeks Seven and Eight: foundations pass two tests and on soft ground stiffness decides; wet ground and pour day close many decisions at once; and the ground slab is a foundation that fails slowly between trades.

Running through all eight weeks is one habit worth keeping. Before any irreversible step, ask who carries the risk if it is wrong, and what written evidence shows that it has been checked. Ask it before signing, before digging, before loading, before pouring and before paying the final account.

The owner's risk is fixed early, in documents and decisions that are cheap to get right and expensive to reverse. Professional sign-off required at every real decision: the licensed specialist named in each lesson.
checklist: Use one monitored groundwater level for uplift, waterproofing and mix design.
Require a readiness review the day before any large pour.
Check that hold-point releases precede the work they cover.
Check point loads at edges and corners, not only mid-panel.
Treat simultaneous defects across buildings as one investigation.
Make records and warranty assignments conditions of final payment.

selftest.q: If you could require only one habit from this whole course on every project, what would it be?
selftest.a: Before any irreversible step, from signing the contract to pouring the mat, ask who carries the risk if it is wrong and what written evidence shows it has been checked. That question, asked while leverage is highest, captures most of the course: delivery and contract terms, investigation, temporary works permits, foundation tests and the records behind a slab.
